title: Gold Extends Breakout on Dollar Weakness; Tesla Jumps on Vegas Robotaxi Clearance

content:

Forex and Precious Metals

According to Seeking Alpha, the precious metal's extended breakout reflects investor appetite for safe-haven assets as confidence in U.S. fiscal management erodes. Dollar weakness typically supports commodity prices denominated in the currency, making gold an attractive hedge for portfolios exposed to currency depreciation risk.

Cryptocurrency

Solana outperformed with a 5.35% advance to $95.02, and BNB climbed 5.07% to $704.90, suggesting selective strength among layer-one and infrastructure tokens. The modest gains across major cryptocurrencies come as traditional macro headwinds—particularly Treasury market volatility and inflation concerns—dominate market sentiment.

Equities and Technology

Tesla's stock jumped following clearance for a Las Vegas robotaxi launch, marking a strategic milestone in the company's autonomous vehicle ambitions. MarketWatch reported the move as a significant step toward commercializing the company's full self-driving capabilities. In the semiconductor space, Coatue Management has opened a new position in AMD stock, signaling renewed confidence in the artificial intelligence trade beyond nvidia's dominant market position. Questions persist about whether international players like IBM can narrow nvidia's AI lead, though competitive dynamics in chip design and deployment remain fluid.

Commodities and Energy

Seeking Alpha reported that Iranian oil supply to China has been constrained by the U.S. blockade, potentially tightening global crude balances. Meanwhile, the Hormuz oil crisis is accelerating global EV adoption, as energy security concerns push both governments and consumers toward electrified transport. Europe's nuclear fleet also faces cooling challenges, according to OilPrice, adding to the continent's energy resilience headwinds.

Macro Policy and Fixed Income

Treasury Department activism is creating market friction as Bessent pursues debt-management initiatives that officials hope will calm fixed-income volatility. However, CNBC reported that his bond strategy is instead stoking inflation concerns, complicating the Fed's inflation-control mandate. The newly activist Treasury approach is undercutting coordination with Federal Reserve leadership, raising questions about policy coherence. Political pressure on the Fed continues, with calls for lower interest rates even as inflation risks persist.

What to Watch

  • Treasury-Fed coordination breakdown: Monitor whether Bessent's fiscal activism and Fed policy continue to diverge, pressuring bond yields and the dollar.
  • Energy supply dynamics: Iranian sanctions tightening and European nuclear constraints could support crude prices and accelerate energy transition investments.
  • Tech leadership in AI: Watch whether AMD and other challengers can gain meaningful share in high-value AI chip segments or if nvidia's dominance persists.

What rescued the week was a pair of earnings reports that the market needed: Amazon reported its highest AWS growth in 18 quarters, and Microsoft's Azure revenue beat estimates while the company guided for growth acceleration, with paid Copilot seats jumping to 30 million from 20 million in a single quarter. Both stocks surged more than 15% post-earnings, and the forced unwind of a heavily leveraged AI-focused hedge fund in the middle of the week likely cleared some of the excess positioning that had weighed on the sector. With 305 S&P 500 companies having now reported, 86% have beaten bottom-line estimates and EPS growth is tracking at 57%, a remarkable underlying earnings cycle that the market is only partially crediting due to macro headwinds.

Rates and the Fed: The Yield Curve Is the Real Story

The Federal Reserve's hold was not the surprise; the bond market's reaction to the accompanying communication was. Yields on the long end spiked in a way that signals investors are repricing not just the pace of cuts but the terminal rate itself, against a backdrop of still-elevated core inflation at 3.3% and US GDP growth that has decelerated to 1.5%. That combination, slowing growth with sticky inflation, is the version of the macro environment that gives the Fed least room to maneuver, and markets are beginning to price that in. Higher-for-longer at the long end is economically restrictive in ways that short rates alone do not capture: mortgage markets, corporate refinancing schedules, and the relative attractiveness of equities versus fixed income all shift when the 30-year sits above 5.25%. For equity investors, the key near-term question is whether the AI earnings cycle is strong enough to sustain current multiples against a rising discount rate. This week's results from Microsoft and Amazon suggest it might be for the mega-cap leaders, but the equal-weight S&P 500 needs yields to stabilize or fall to sustain its own methodical uptrend.

Oil and the Iran Conflict: The Persistent Premium

WTI crude ended the week down approximately 4.7%, with front-month September futures last seen near $85 per barrel, after the US and Iran briefly agreed to pause strikes before US Central Command intercepted a surprise Iranian attack and hostilities resumed. The week's oil price action illustrates the structural dynamic now at work: any diplomatic signal brings immediate relief selling, but the absence of a durable resolution means that relief is shallow and temporary. An $85 per barrel oil price is not catastrophic for global growth, but it is high enough to keep inflation sticky, complicate central bank communication, and impose a meaningful terms-of-trade burden on oil-importing economies including Pakistan. For Saudi Arabia, elevated oil revenue supports fiscal stability but prolonged regional tension raises cost, logistics, and financing risks for listed corporates. The energy sector's 11.3% YTD gain on the Saudi exchange reflects the fiscal tailwind, but it also illustrates why the broader Tadawul is struggling: the market knows that the same conflict driving energy revenues is simultaneously weighing on almost every other sector.

Saudi Equities (TASI): Technical Deterioration, Valuation Offers Little Near-Term Comfort

The Tadawul All-Share Index closed the week at 10,590, down 1.98% week-on-week, reversing the prior week's modest recovery and falling back below its 20-day moving average near 10,750. What makes this week's decline more concerning than the one before it is that weekly traded value rose 10.34% to SAR 20.6 billion, meaning sellers were not simply absent buyers but active participants. The RSI on a 14-day basis has fallen back to approximately 33, directional indicators show the downside trend regaining strength with ADX near 32 and negative DI well above positive DI, and the Bollinger lower band has converged with the closing price around 10,590. The immediate support level to watch is 10,550: a decisive break below that level opens the path toward 10,450. Recovery requires first reclaiming 10,650 to 10,730, and then clearing 10,850 before the picture shifts from negative to neutral. At a TASI-level P/E of 16.5x and P/B of 2.1x, valuation is not providing a floor in the current environment. The sector breakdown shows the week's pain was concentrated in Insurance (down 7.4%), Capital Goods (down 6.3%), and Materials (down 3.8%), while Healthcare and Consumer Staples posted small positive weeks, suggesting selective defensive rotation rather than a broad recovery trade.

Pakistan Equities (KSE-100): The Standout Performer, With Caveats

The KSE-100 closed the week at 176,094, up 3.0% week-on-week and up a remarkable 5,073 points in absolute terms, driven by a combination of geopolitical relief early in the week, strong June 2026 corporate earnings, and a series of positive macro datapoints. The SBP held its policy rate unchanged at 11.5%, a decision that was fully in line with expectations and had minimal market impact. More materially, Saudi Arabia's rollover of its US$5 billion deposit for a further three years directly reduces Pakistan's FY27 external debt repayments to US$21.5 billion, a meaningful reduction in near-term refinancing risk. The Pakistani rupee remained broadly stable at 277.80 per dollar, and ADTV surged 48.5% to 1.3 billion shares, suggesting genuine participation rather than thin-volume drift. The brownfield refinery policy amendment extending fiscal incentive windows from six to seven years and unlocking a potential $6 billion investment plan adds a structural positive for the sector. With the KSE-100 trading at a forward P/E of approximately 7.8x and a year-end target of 263,800 implied by the current earnings trajectory, the risk-reward here remains among the more compelling in our emerging market coverage, though geopolitical resolution, particularly on US-Iran and its knock-on effect on oil prices and regional sentiment, remains the swing factor.

Crypto: Consolidation Beneath Key Levels

Bitcoin closed the week near $63,036, essentially flat on a seven-day basis and well below the $65,000 level that had briefly offered a foothold in late July. Ethereum sits at $1,856, down from the $1,967 level reached earlier in the week, and Solana trades near $72.92. The broader crypto picture this week reflects the same macro headwinds weighing on risk assets generally: rising Treasury yields reduce the opportunity cost of not holding yield-bearing instruments, and uncertainty around the US growth trajectory and oil prices creates a risk-off undertone that tends to weigh disproportionately on high-beta assets. Bitcoin's failure to sustain above $65,000 in the face of strong hyperscaler earnings, which historically would have been a risk-on catalyst, suggests the asset class is consolidating after a period of positioning excess rather than embarking on a directional leg. Until yields stabilize and the Iran situation shows a durable de-escalation, the path of least resistance for crypto looks sideways to modestly lower.

This Week's Recommendations

  • KSE-100: Accumulate selectively, bias toward energy and banking names. At a forward P/E of 7.8x with a credible path to 263,800 by year-end, Pakistan equities offer among the best risk-adjusted upside in our coverage. The Saudi deposit rollover reduces near-term external financing risk materially. Within the market, OGDC, PPL, UBL, HBL, and FFC stand out on a combination of earnings momentum, dividend support, and reasonable valuations. We would add on any pullback toward the 170,000 to 172,000 range.
  • TASI: Remain underweight, watch 10,550 as the critical floor. The technical picture has deteriorated with higher-volume selling, RSI near 33, and the index pressing against its Bollinger lower band at the close. A break below 10,550 would open downside toward 10,450. We would not add exposure until TASI closes above 10,730 on sustained volume. Within the market, the healthcare and consumer staples sectors, the only two posting positive weeks, offer relative defensiveness if regional investors need Saudi exposure.
  • US Mega-Cap Tech: Hold core positions, do not chase the post-earnings spike. The AI monetization signal from Amazon and Microsoft is genuine and meaningful, and the forced deleveraging from the mid-week hedge fund unwind likely cleared the most extreme positioning. However, with the 30-year Treasury yield at 5.27%, the discount rate environment is unfavorable for multiples expansion. We would hold existing positions in AMZN and MSFT but wait for a yield stabilization signal before adding aggressively, as seasonality turns historically more challenging in August and September.
  • Oil and Energy: Reduce tactical length, maintain strategic exposure. With WTI near $85 per barrel and the Iran conflict driving a persistent risk premium rather than a spike-and-fade dynamic, we see limited upside from current levels without a material escalation. The Saudi energy sector's 11.3% YTD gain already prices in much of the fiscal benefit. We would trim tactical oil longs established at lower levels and maintain only strategic energy exposure through names with strong balance sheets and dividend coverage.
  • Bitcoin: Neutral, no new position. BTC at $63,036 is consolidating but lacks a near-term catalyst to break higher in the current macro context. Elevated yields, unresolved Iran risk, and the absence of a new institutional demand driver argue for patience. We would revisit the thesis if BTC reclaims $65,500 on strong volume or if the macro backdrop shifts meaningfully in favor of risk assets.

What to Watch Next Week

The week ahead is dense with data and events that could shift the picture across multiple asset classes. Friday's US nonfarm payrolls report is the single most important data release: in an environment where the Fed is holding on sticky inflation but growth is slowing to 1.5%, a strong jobs number reinforces the higher-for-longer yield narrative while a weak one reopens the growth concern. Average hourly earnings and the unemployment rate will be equally scrutinized. Earlier in the week, Monday's ISM Manufacturing Index and Wednesday's ISM Non-Manufacturing Index will offer a read on whether the growth deceleration is broadening beyond GDP into the real economy. The Bank of Japan's monetary policy meeting spanning July 30th and 31st carries implications for global rate differentials and yen-funded carry trades, which have been a source of volatility in Asian equity markets, particularly after the KOSPI's dramatic swings this week. On earnings, AMD reports Tuesday and is the next meaningful data point for AI semiconductor demand following the mixed signals of the past month. Eli Lilly on Wednesday adds a high-profile read on healthcare and GLP-1 demand trends. In Pakistan, the market will continue monitoring June quarter results from major corporates, with the banking sector in particular likely to drive sentiment given its weight in the index. And across all markets, any diplomatic development, positive or negative, in the US-Iran conflict remains the highest-impact potential catalyst of the week: a credible ceasefire framework would immediately reprice oil, regional equities, and risk appetite globally, while a further escalation, particularly involving the Strait of Hormuz, would do the opposite.

The SPX has slipped below its 50-day simple moving average, and the Nasdaq is trading beneath near-term support at 25,000. The technical setup leans moderately bearish into next week unless a meaningful geopolitical de-escalation materializes.

Oil and Energy: Two Chokepoints in Play

The energy market is now pricing two simultaneous disruption risks rather than one. The Strait of Hormuz remains the primary concern following twelve consecutive nights of US strikes on Iranian military targets, but the Houthi declaration of a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia and claimed strikes on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea have brought Bab el-Mandeb back into the threat calculus. Brent's intraweek peak above $101 represents a structurally important psychological threshold, and while the pullback to $97 was real, it was catalyzed entirely by diplomacy speculation rather than any change in supply conditions. WTI crude September futures were last seen near $88.86 at Thursday's close, down 3.6% on the day, attributable to the Islamabad back-channel reports. The risk here is asymmetric: diplomatic progress could bring a sharp correction in crude, but any escalation into Saudi infrastructure brings a price spike that would be difficult to contain. Pakistan's LNG spot purchase at $21.88 per mmbtu, the highest since March 2026, is an early read on where regional energy import costs are heading.

Saudi Arabia (TASI): Cautious-Neutral, Watching 10,850

TASI closed the week at 10,804, up 84 points or 0.78% week-on-week, recovering from an early-week test near 10,650 and reclaiming both the 10,750 level and the 20-day moving average near 10,790. That recovery is meaningful, but the index remains below the critical 10,850 resistance zone, and the technical picture is best characterized as cautious-neutral rather than bullish. The 14-day RSI has recovered to around 46 from near 33 the previous week, which is improvement, but both the 14-day and 30-day RSI remain below the neutral 50 threshold. Volume profile analysis places the Point of Control at 11,025, a distant target given current resistance density up to 10,850. Among sectors, Software and Services (+4.1%) and Utilities (+3.9%) led on the week, while Transportation (-3.0%), Consumer Durables (-3.0%), and Consumer Discretionary (-2.7%) lagged. The Houthi naval blockade declaration and claimed tanker strikes in the Red Sea are a direct geopolitical risk to Saudi Arabia that goes beyond oil prices, potentially affecting maritime insurance costs and Red Sea shipping flows. A clean, volume-backed close above 10,850 would open the path toward 10,950-10,975, but failure there refocuses attention on 10,650 support.

Pakistan Equities (KSE-100): Pressure, Value, and a Diplomatic Wildcard

The KSE-100 declined 2.7% week-on-week to close at 171,021 points, with average daily turnover contracting 3.2% to 881.4 million shares. The pressure was broad-based, driven by geopolitical anxiety and rising oil import costs, though pockets of strength emerged in Refinery (+5.5%), Insurance (+2.5%), and Textile Spinning (+1.1%). The worst performers were Jute (-10.9%), Sugar and Allied Industries (-8.0%), and Close-end Mutual Funds (-6.6%). At the stock level, the gas distribution names were notably hard hit: SSGC fell 14.1% and SNGP 8.6%, reflecting concerns around higher input costs and tariff uncertainty as OGRA transitions to daily petroleum price-setting. Against this backdrop, two offsetting positives deserve weight. S&P Global upgraded Pakistan's long-term sovereign credit rating to B with a stable outlook, citing reform momentum, and Pakistan is actively brokering US-Iran talks, a role that carries both diplomatic capital and potential economic dividend if negotiations progress. T-bill yields rose 12-51 basis points across tenors at the latest auction, a signal that markets are pricing in a status-quo or cautious MPC, even as the disinflationary trend and a comfortable external account position argue for eventual rate relief. The index's current P/E of 7.8x remains deeply attractive on a regional and historical basis, and a KSE-100 target of 263,800 by December 2026 implies substantial upside if macro risks stabilize.

Pakistan Macro and Sector Detail: Banks, Fertilizer, Energy

Banking sector deposits grew 15.2% year-on-year to PkR 40.9 trillion as of June 2026, a strong headline that supports the sector's asset growth story even as net interest margins face compression from the policy rate environment. UBL's second-quarter results illustrate the dynamic clearly: quarterly net profit came in at PkR 37.5 billion (EPS PkR 15.0), up 31% year-on-year but down 23% quarter-on-quarter, with NII declining 1% year-on-year as deposit repricing outpaced earning asset growth. Deposits surged 43% year-on-year to a record PkR 6.1 trillion, which is a franchise story, not a margin story. The fertilizer sector presents a cleaner near-term picture: urea offtakes rose 2% year-on-year to 592,000 tons in June, supported by Kharif season demand, subsidies, and cheaper financing, while DAP sales fell 58% year-on-year on pricing. Hydrocarbon production data shows oil output stable at approximately 71,344 barrels per day and gas at 3,005 mmcfd, with sequential softness at several fields partially offset by gains at Makori East and Qadirpur. Pakistan's request for a $10 billion bilateral exchange stabilization facility from the US adds a geopolitical dimension to the macro story that could prove significant if the Islamabad diplomatic track on Iran gains traction.

Crypto: Range-Bound but Resilient

Bitcoin closed the week near $64,674, up approximately 0.77% over the past 24 hours and broadly range-bound between $63,800 and $66,200 across the week's sessions. Ethereum showed relative strength at $1,912, up 2.34%, while Solana traded near $75 and BNB near $573. The pattern across the week was consistent: crypto acted as a mild risk-off hedge when Middle East tensions spiked, but lacked the conviction to break decisively higher. The ECB's evolving rate path, which has shifted toward a more cautious posture given energy and inflation uncertainty from Hormuz disruption, is creating a modestly supportive backdrop for digital assets in Europe-facing flows, though this has not yet translated into a sustained bid. Bitcoin's inability to hold above $66,000 despite genuine geopolitical anxiety suggests the market is waiting for cleaner macro signals, likely from the FOMC meeting and the next round of PCE data, before committing to a directional move.

This Week's Recommendations

  • Pakistan equities, selective accumulation: At a P/E of 7.8x and with a credible December 2026 index target implying meaningful upside, the KSE-100 offers value that is difficult to ignore at current levels. We favor names with direct leverage to macro normalization: OGDC and PPL for energy exposure, UBL, MEBL, and HBL in banking given the deposit growth story, and FFC in fertilizers given stable Kharif-driven demand and high dividend yield. Position sizing should reflect the oil-price and geopolitical sensitivity of Pakistan's import bill, with a clear stop on further deterioration in the US-Iran situation.
  • TASI, tactical hold with a trigger: TASI's recovery to 10,804 is encouraging but insufficient to shift our stance to outright bullish. We hold current positions and add exposure only on a confirmed, volume-backed close above 10,850. If that level clears cleanly, the path to 10,950-10,975 becomes the base case. The Houthi-Saudi risk is a local amplifier worth monitoring: any credible strike on Saudi oil infrastructure would move TASI sharply, and the Energy sector (+12.9% YTD) may see profit-taking on de-escalation while Banks (+3.0% YTD, 11.2x P/E) offer more defensible relative value.
  • Crude oil, remain exposed but hedge the downside: The structural case for elevated oil is intact as long as both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb remain under threat. However, the diplomatic signal from Islamabad is real, and a ceasefire announcement over the weekend would send WTI sharply lower from $88.86. We maintain oil exposure for its inflation-hedging properties but recommend tight trailing stops given the binary nature of the de-escalation risk. Pakistani refinery stocks, which rose 5.5% this week, are a partial regional proxy for this trade.
  • US tech, cautious ahead of Mag-7 earnings: The SPX below its 50-day SMA and the Nasdaq below 25,000 support are technically meaningful signals. With Amazon, Apple, Meta, and Microsoft all reporting this week, and with Alphabet having already shown the market's impatience with CapEx intensity, we recommend reducing exposure to high-multiple AI-adjacent names ahead of results and re-evaluating on the actual guidance prints. The underlying earnings season is strong at 87% bottom-line beat rate, but macro headwinds from oil and yields are real offsets.
  • Bitcoin, neutral with a downside watch on FOMC: With BTC range-bound near $64,674 and the FOMC meeting on Tuesday-Wednesday representing the week's biggest macro binary, we hold a neutral stance. A hawkish surprise from the Fed, particularly if PCE comes in warm on Thursday, could compress crypto alongside risk assets broadly. A dovish hold or any Iran de-escalation signal would likely support a retest of the $66,000 area. We see limited asymmetry for new long positions until one of these catalysts resolves.

What to Watch Next Week

The week ahead is one of the most catalyst-dense of the year. The FOMC decision on Wednesday is the central macro event: markets will parse every word of the statement for signals on the September meeting, particularly in the context of rising oil prices and a Services PMI that just hit an eight-month high. Thursday brings Q2 GDP (advance reading), PCE prices, personal income, and personal spending, collectively the most complete snapshot of the US consumer and inflation picture available ahead of the September FOMC. On the earnings front, four of the Magnificent Seven report in a single week: Meta and Microsoft on Wednesday, Amazon and Apple on Thursday. Given Alphabet's CapEx-driven selloff, CapEx guidance from all four will be as important as EPS. The Bank of Japan's monetary policy meeting runs Thursday-Friday, and any signal of further normalization would add to global yield pressure. Geopolitically, the Pakistan-brokered US-Iran exploratory discussions are the single highest-impact wildcard: progress over the weekend could reset oil, yields, and risk appetite for the entire week, while failure or escalation, particularly any US "massive attack" on Iran as discussed publicly, would drive the opposite. Pakistan's MPC meeting is also on the horizon, with the decision between status quo and a cut carrying meaningful implications for KSE-100 sentiment and bank NIM trajectories. Monday's US Durable Orders and Tuesday's Consumer Confidence round out a schedule that leaves very little room for markets to drift without fresh information.

title: Iran Shock Meets Earnings Season: The Week That Reset Global Risk Pricing
excerpt: A U.S.-Iran escalation drove oil up 14%, rattled global equities, and forced a fundamental reassessment of risk across every market in our coverage.
content:
The week ending 19 July 2026 was defined by a single geopolitical shock rippling across every asset class and geography in our coverage universe. The U.S. resumption of strikes against Iran following the collapse of the ceasefire pushed WTI crude up 14% on the week, with Brent spot breaching $83 per barrel at one point. That single move cascaded into a semiconductor selloff in New York, a three-week losing streak on the Saudi exchange, a sharp pullback on the KSE-100 in Karachi, and a Fed that finds itself watching oil prices instead of wage data. Beneath the geopolitical noise, however, Q2 earnings in the U.S. are tracking well above expectations, and several emerging market equity markets are sitting at valuations that have historically rewarded patience. The picture this week is one of compressed risk premiums meeting an expanding tail risk, and the appropriate response is selectivity, not paralysis.

Global Macro: Iran, Oil, and the Fed's Narrowing Room

The cancellation of the U.S.-Iran ceasefire and six consecutive days of American strikes against Iranian targets have reset the geopolitical baseline for the second half of 2026. WTI crude's 14% weekly surge to above $82 per barrel, and Brent's move above $83, are not merely an energy story. Sustained oil prices at these levels feed directly into headline inflation figures, which complicates the Federal Reserve's already delicate positioning. At its June meeting the Fed held rates at 3.5% to 3.75%, with the FOMC internally split between holds and hikes. This week's CPI and PPI figures surprised to the downside, offering a brief window of relief, but the subsequent oil move may well absorb that relief before the July 29 meeting even arrives. Our read is that rate cuts are firmly off the table for 2026, and the bar for hikes remains high but is no longer as remote as it appeared two weeks ago. Investors entering the week of 20 July should treat the Fed meeting on 29 July as a secondary catalyst, with oil and Iran as the primary variable setting the floor and ceiling for risk appetite globally.

U.S. Equities: Strong Earnings, Fragile Sentiment

The S&P 500 slipped just over 1% on the week, a modest headline decline that understates the internal violence playing out in technology and semiconductors. The SOX Semiconductor Index is now down approximately 20% from its June highs, though it remains up roughly 64% year-to-date, a reminder that recent pain is occurring within the context of a still-powerful structural rally. The drivers of the semiconductor pullback are layered: SK Hynix posted its largest single-day decline in history after profit estimates were cut, AI compression technology from PrismML and earlier Google TurboQuant research raised questions about long-term memory demand intensity, and Chinese startup Moonshot AI unveiled a new open-weight model claiming to rival OpenAI and Anthropic at lower cost. Collectively, these developments shifted the market from a "buy the AI story" posture to a "verify the AI economics" posture. The good news is that Q2 earnings are tracking sharply above expectations, with 76% of the 47 S&P 500 companies that have reported beating on revenue and 95% beating on the bottom line, with earnings growth tracking at over 52% year-over-year. The key test arrives Wednesday 22 July when Alphabet reports: CapEx guidance from that report will either reaffirm or destabilize the broader AI infrastructure trade for the rest of the summer. We would characterize the U.S. equity setup as "cautiously constructive on earnings, watching oil," and would not add aggressively to semiconductor exposure ahead of Alphabet's print.

Saudi Arabia: TASI Tests Lower Band as Selling Pressure Persists

The Tadawul All-Share Index extended its decline for a third consecutive week, closing at 10,720, down 0.82% week-on-week, and sitting at only 33% of its 52-week range. Weekly traded value fell to SAR 17.9 billion, an 8.7% decline from the prior week, which is a double-edged signal: lighter turnover tempers the case for aggressive distribution, but declining participation in a falling market rarely indicates accumulation. The index is now trading below its 20-day moving average near 10,850, and that level has flipped from support to resistance. The volume profile is thin between current levels and the next support zone at 10,650 and 10,550, meaning a sentiment deterioration could move through those levels faster than the headline distance implies. The 14-day RSI sits near 33, approaching but not yet at oversold territory, while the directional indicators show the downside trend gaining strength with ADX rising to around 28. Sector performance was almost uniformly negative this week, with Capital Goods leading losses at 4%, Utilities down 3.9%, and Media and Entertainment down 3.2%. Energy, which might be expected to benefit from the oil price surge, was essentially flat at -0.1%, suggesting that the geopolitical risk premium is being discounted against lower volume expectations. With Q2 reporting season approaching, company-level commentary on Iran war exposure to volumes, costs, and margins will be the next meaningful catalyst for the index. A recovery above 10,850 is needed before TASI's technical picture turns anything other than cautious.

Pakistan: KSE-100 Absorbs a Geopolitical Shock, Fundamentals Offer a Floor

The KSE-100 closed at 175,803 points, down 6,439 points or 3.5% on the week, after an extraordinary two-day decline of 8,723 points driven directly by U.S.-Iran escalation fears, including the threatened U.S. strike on Iranian energy facilities. A mid-week recovery followed after President Trump signaled openness to negotiations and reportedly withdrew a proposed 20% transit fee on the Strait of Hormuz, but renewed tensions in the back half of the week erased much of that recovery. Average daily trading volumes fell 29% week-on-week to around 911 million shares, a sign that investors are reducing exposure rather than repositioning. The macro backdrop adds complexity: the current account posted a deficit of $139 million in FY26 versus a $1.8 billion surplus in the prior year, FX reserves declined by $1.2 billion to $17.2 billion due to debt repayments, and the trade deficit widened sharply to $4.7 billion in June alone. Set against this, the positives are real: auto sales grew 33% year-on-year to 244,000 units in FY26, IT exports hit a record high of $4.6 billion, and LSM industrial output rose 6% year-on-year over eleven months. The index now trades at a forward P/E of approximately 7.6x to 8.1x depending on the earnings baseline used, a valuation that is historically attractive and compares favorably to every regional peer in our data. The Pakistani rupee held steady at around PKR 277.96 per dollar. Our conviction names remain energy and banking oriented, with E&P plays, major commercial banks, and select cement and fertilizer stocks offering the best risk-reward at current levels. The short-term trajectory hinges almost entirely on the Iran negotiation timeline.

Commodities: Oil Dominates, Gold Softens, Coal Steady

Crude oil was the week's defining commodity, with Brent spot settling near $83 per barrel, up almost 12% on the week, and WTI futures for August delivery adding approximately 14%. The Iran conflict risk premium is now embedded in the curve, and any de-escalation signal would likely produce a sharp reversal, as it did briefly mid-week in Pakistan equities when Trump's negotiation comments moved markets. Gold, which might have been expected to benefit from geopolitical risk, actually fell 3% on the week to just under $3,995 per troy ounce, likely reflecting some profit-taking after its extraordinary year-to-date performance and a brief firming of real rate expectations on the back of the oil move. Coal was essentially unchanged at $106.40 per metric ton. Cotton edged up 1% to $90.65 per pound. The commodity picture this week reinforces a consistent theme: geopolitical risk is being priced narrowly into energy rather than broadly into safe havens, which suggests markets still believe the conflict remains containable. That assumption deserves scrutiny heading into next week.

Crypto: Consolidation, Not Capitulation

Bitcoin ended the week at $64,459, up a modest 0.54% in the latest 24-hour window, after trading as low as $62,655 mid-week when risk sentiment was at its most stressed. Ethereum at $1,872 and Solana at $76.26 both showed mild positive momentum in the final sessions, consistent with the broader pattern of crypto finding a floor during equity market volatility rather than amplifying it, a behavioral shift that has become more consistent over the past several months. The week's crypto story is one of resilience rather than strength: digital assets absorbed the Iran shock, the semiconductor rout, and a down week in U.S. equities without a significant drawdown. The ECB's ongoing reassessment of its rate path amid Hormuz tensions, covered across our daily briefs this week, adds a secondary macro overlay for crypto, as European rate expectations feed into dollar strength dynamics and, indirectly, into Bitcoin's denominator. We do not view the current $64,000 to $65,000 range as a launchpad in either direction without a resolution to the broader macro uncertainty. Accumulation at current levels is defensible for investors with a medium-term horizon; momentum-driven entries are harder to justify this week.

This Week's Recommendations

  • KSE-100 E&P sector, Pakistan (OGDC, PPL): At a market P/E below 8x and with oil prices elevated, Pakistan's exploration and production companies carry an unusual combination of macro tailwind from higher commodity prices and deep valuation support. Both names have been consistent top picks across our coverage, and the week's selloff has widened the discount further. Accumulate on weakness with a December 2026 target horizon.
  • PSO, Pakistan OMCs: Full-year FY26 earnings for the sector are tracking 17% year-on-year growth, and FY27 brings two additional catalysts: pending regulated margin revisions and volumetric recovery from improving consumer mobility. The December 2026 target price of PKR 900 for PSO implies meaningful upside from current levels. The short-term headwind from inventory losses in Q4 FY26 is known and, in our view, already reflected in the price.
  • INDU, Pakistan Autos: Auto sales grew 33% year-on-year in FY26, driven by stable prices, lower financing rates, and OEM discount offers. While lower import duties introduce competitive pressure, INDU's scale and brand positioning provide a buffer. A 10.4% dividend yield for FY26 provides income support while waiting for the re-rating. The December 2026 target price implies over 100% upside, which appropriately reflects the risk, but the dividend alone justifies the position for income-oriented portfolios.
  • U.S. Large-Cap Technology (selective, post-Alphabet earnings): We would not add broadly to tech ahead of the Wednesday 22 July Alphabet print. However, if Alphabet confirms or raises its full-year CapEx range of $180 to $190 billion and reports strong cloud and advertising revenues, the conditions for a tactical re-entry into AI infrastructure and software names will materially improve. Microsoft and Salesforce have already begun to recover while semiconductor hardware names lag, and that rotation within tech may deepen.
  • Saudi TASI (tactical, not structural): A three-week losing streak with RSI approaching 33 and a thin volume profile below 10,650 creates the conditions for a tactical bounce, particularly if oil stabilizes or Iran headlines moderate. A confirmed close back above 10,750 would open a test of 10,850, the key stabilization level. We would not treat this as a structural re-entry below 10,850: the trend remains downward and the directional indicators confirm it. Position sizing should reflect that this is a mean-reversion trade within a weak trend, not a trend reversal.

What to Watch Next Week

The week of 20 July carries a light economic calendar in the United States but an exceptionally heavy earnings slate, and the contrast between those two facts defines the market dynamic heading in. Wednesday 22 July is the pivotal session: Alphabet reports after the close, and its CapEx guidance will function as a referendum on the AI investment cycle for the rest of the summer. Tesla also reports Wednesday, adding a consumer and industrial technology dimension to the same session. On Thursday, Intel and Lockheed Martin report, providing a read on both the AI infrastructure supply chain and defense spending in an environment where U.S. military activity has increased. Broader earnings context: S&P 500 year-over-year growth is tracking at approximately 23% to 25%, and that bar must be cleared by the majority of the remaining reporters to sustain current index valuations. On the macro side, the July 29 Federal Reserve meeting is the horizon event, but next week's EIA crude inventory figures on Wednesday and natural gas inventories on Thursday will be watched for any supply-side response to the Iran conflict. In Pakistan, listed company financial results for June 2026 will begin arriving in earnest, and those earnings will be the local market's best counterweight to geopolitical pressure. In Saudi Arabia, Q2 company reports will begin offering the first concrete evidence of how the Iran war is affecting regional corporate margins and volumes. Finally, and most critically: any diplomatic development on the U.S.-Iran front, in either direction, remains the single highest-impact variable across every market in our coverage universe this week.

title: Oil Shock Absorbed, AI Holds the Wheel: Cross-Market Weekly Outlook
excerpt: Geopolitics rattled markets but AI earnings, record Pakistan remittances, and Q2 optimism kept the broader trend intact heading into a pivotal data week.
content:
The week ending July 10 delivered a clear message: geopolitics can move markets, but they cannot hold them. The collapse of the U.S.-Iran ceasefire sent oil briefly to $80 per barrel, knocked the KSE-100 down more than 4,600 points intraday, and pushed U.S. Treasury yields to their highest levels since mid-May. Yet by Friday, equities on both sides of the Atlantic were recovering, the VIX had retreated to 15, and the S&P 500 was posting its second consecutive weekly gain. The dominant story is not the conflict itself but the market's evolving immune response to it: AI earnings momentum, record remittances, and a powerful Q2 earnings setup are proving more durable than headline risk.

U.S. Equities: AI Momentum Absorbs the Geopolitical Shock

The S&P 500 gained 1.3% on the week, closing at 7,575, and the NASDAQ added 1.7% to 26,281, even as oil spiked and bond yields climbed. The composition of that gain tells the real story. Information technology rose 3.4% and communication services added 2.4%, while defensives and rate-sensitive sectors lagged: healthcare fell 1.8%, materials dropped 2.2%, and utilities slid 0.8%. Large-cap growth is where the conviction sits right now, with the YTD spread between large-cap growth and small-cap growth now running at roughly 13 percentage points. The Dow, by contrast, slipped 0.5% for the week, weighed down by its more industrial and consumer-staples-heavy composition. With Q2 earnings season opening on July 14, analysts are pencilling in 23.6% year-over-year earnings growth for the S&P 500, the second consecutive quarter above 20%, and estimates were actually revised higher during the quarter, which is rare and significant. Technology alone is expected to deliver 63% earnings growth and the highest revenue growth of any sector. The bar is elevated, and any shortfall from the mega-caps will be punished, but the underlying fundamental case remains intact.

U.S. Fixed Income and the Fed: Warsh's First Test

Treasury yields moved meaningfully higher this week, with the 10-year finishing at 4.56%, up from 4.37% two weeks earlier, and the 30-year crossing 5.06%. The bond market is pricing a world where the Fed stays on hold but cannot cut: oil is elevated, services ISM came in at 54.0%, and the June FOMC minutes revealed that a few committee members felt there was already sufficient evidence to hike at the June 16-17 meeting. The 2-10 spread has compressed to 36 basis points from 68 at year-end, a flattening that reflects mounting concern about the inflation trajectory rather than growth optimism. The critical event next week is Tuesday's CPI print and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first semiannual testimony before Congress, followed by PPI on Wednesday. Warsh has deliberately reduced the Fed's forward guidance cadence, which makes the testimony a higher-information event than usual. If CPI surprises to the upside and Warsh signals any tolerance for a rate hike, the Treasury selloff could extend rapidly. Duration risk is real and we remain cautious on intermediate-to-long Treasuries until the inflation picture clarifies.

Oil, Iran, and the Hormuz Equation

Crude's week-long arc captures the tension well. WTI briefly touched $80 per barrel mid-week as Iran resumed attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. launched retaliatory airstrikes, before retreating toward $71 by Friday, still up 4.0% on the week and up a remarkable 49.9% year-to-date. Saudi Arabia's decision to make its largest oil price cut in decades adds a structural counterweight: OPEC is clearly willing to defend market share even as geopolitical risk pushes spot prices higher. Pakistan's government simultaneously moved to buy more LNG as Hormuz flows failed to fully recover, illustrating how the supply disruption has real downstream consequences for import-dependent emerging markets. The key distinction for equity investors is that the market's sensitivity to oil spikes has diminished. In March, the S&P 500 fell on 10 of 12 days when WTI rose more than 3%; from April through June that fell to 8 of 12 days with a much smaller average decline. Oil above $80 on a sustained basis would change the calculus for the Fed and corporate margins, but at current levels the earnings and AI narratives retain the upper hand.

Pakistan: Macro Strength Battles Geopolitical Noise

The KSE-100 closed the week at 182,242 points, down 3,130 points or 1.7% week-on-week, masking the severity of the intraday move: the index shed 4,626 points on Wednesday alone before Trump's comments at the NATO summit that the conflict would not escalate provided partial relief. The macro backdrop, however, remains genuinely constructive. FY26 worker remittances hit a record $41.6 billion, up 9% year-on-year, and SBP foreign exchange reserves climbed $1.9 billion to $18.5 billion as of July 3. T-bill yields fell 31-40 basis points across all tenors at the first FY27 auction, confirming that the monetary easing cycle has room to run. Cement dispatches for FY26 reached 50.5 million tons, a four-year high driven by a 9% recovery in domestic volumes as lower policy rates feed through to construction activity. The cement sector's profitability is expected to rise 21% year-on-year in the fourth quarter on higher retention prices. Meanwhile, the removal of the Minimum Deposit Rate restriction for private sector deposits and high-balance individual accounts gives banks meaningful pricing flexibility. The index trades at a forward P/E of roughly 7.7-8.4 times with a dividend yield around 6.0%, among the cheapest in Asia on both metrics. Our conviction picks in this market are OGDC, PPL, UBL, MEBL, HBL, FFC, PSO, LUCK, and FCCL.

Saudi Arabia: TASI Holds Support but Sellers Remain in Control

TASI closed the week at 10,808, off a marginal 19 points or 0.17%, but the technical picture is more fragile than that headline suggests. Weekly traded value fell 9.7% to SAR 19.6 billion, indicating that the easing of selling pressure reflected buyer exhaustion rather than genuine demand recovery. The index sits at roughly 39% of its 52-week range, the 14-day RSI is near 37, and directional indicators show the negative trend gaining structure with ADX rising to around 25. The critical near-term level is 10,900-10,950: that range represents both the 20-day moving average and the key volume resistance cluster, and the market has consistently failed to reclaim it. A confirmed close above 10,950 on expanding volume would be the first signal that buyers are regaining control; failure at that level keeps the bias negative toward 10,750 and then 10,650. At the sector level, Energy (+2.3%) and Pharma (+0.5%) were the week's only meaningful bright spots, while Insurance (-3.8%), Media (-4.0%), Consumer Staples Distribution (-3.6%), and Transportation (-2.8%) led declines. Saudi Aramco gained 2.4% on the week, contributing to the Energy sector's outperformance as the geopolitical bid in oil supported upstream names.

Semiconductors and the AI Hardware Cycle

The SK Hynix Nasdaq debut, raising $26.5 billion in what is shaping up as one of the largest listings of 2026, is the most significant structural event in global capital markets this week. It arrives at an awkward moment: the KOSPI, which at one point had doubled year-to-date on AI hardware enthusiasm, has since fallen 20% from its peak into bear market territory, and the PHLX Semiconductor Index ended the week testing its 50-day moving average after a choppy performance. Samsung's earlier profit surge of 1,800% year-on-year on AI-driven memory demand underscored the fundamental case, but the market is clearly becoming more discerning about which companies in the AI supply chain are translating revenue into durable earnings. Taiwan's market fell 3.5% for the week, and ASML reports Wednesday followed by TSMC on Thursday, making those two prints the semiconductor sector's true stress test for the week ahead. The core thesis remains intact: AI infrastructure spending is accelerating, memory demand is structurally elevated, and earnings revisions are positive. But volatility at this stage of the cycle is a feature of maturation, not a sign of collapse.

Digital Assets: Range-Bound with Macro Sensitivity

Bitcoin oscillated through the week, touching $64,332 on Thursday before retreating to $63,940 on Saturday and sitting at $64,104 as of this writing, down 0.33% over the past 24 hours. Ethereum and Solana are similarly soft, with ETH at $1,818 and SOL at $77.41. The pattern across the week reflects Bitcoin's increasing sensitivity to macro variables rather than crypto-specific catalysts: the mid-week spike in oil and Treasury yields that pressured risk assets weighed on crypto, while the subsequent equity recovery provided partial support. China's diverging inflation data, with producer deflation persisting even as consumer prices tick modestly higher, has been a recurring backdrop influence given its implications for global liquidity conditions. Bitcoin remains comfortably above the $62,500 support level that held through the geopolitical sell-off, and the range of $62,000-$65,000 now represents the consolidation band to monitor. A confirmed break above $65,000 on meaningful volume would open the path toward the next resistance cluster, while a failure at current levels with deteriorating macro news could retest the low-$60,000s.

This Week's Recommendations

  • Pakistan E&P (OGDC, PPL): Overweight. E&P sector earnings are projected to rise 32% year-on-year in Q4 FY26 on higher oil and gas production, with domestic oil output up 6% week-on-week to 70,157 barrels per day. SBP reserves at $18.5 billion and record remittances underpin the macro floor. OGDC and PPL remain the highest-conviction names at current valuations, with the KSE-100's forward P/E below 8x offering meaningful upside to a December target of 263,800 on the index.
  • Pakistan Cement (LUCK, FCCL): Overweight. FY26 dispatches hit a four-year high of 50.5 million tons, Q4 profitability is expected to rise 21% on pricing power, and the monetary easing cycle continues to support domestic construction demand. LUCK (target PkR735) and FCCL (target PkR88) are the preferred vehicles.
  • U.S. Large-Cap Technology: Maintain exposure, complement with cyclicals. With S&P 500 tech earnings expected at 63% growth for Q2 and estimates revised higher during the quarter, the fundamental case is not broken. However, given elevated valuations and semiconductor volatility, pair core tech exposure with industrials (up 18% YTD) and communication services (2.4% this week) to reduce concentration risk ahead of a potentially volatile reporting season.
  • U.S. Duration: Reduce or hedge. The 30-year Treasury at 5.06% and a Fed chair who has signaled tolerance for rate hikes if inflation persists means the risk-reward on long-duration bonds is unfavorable into Tuesday's CPI and Warsh testimony. Short-duration or floating-rate instruments are preferable until the inflation trajectory clarifies.
  • TASI: Neutral, tactical only above 10,950. TASI's technical setup remains negative below 10,900-10,950. Any position should be conditional on a confirmed close above that band. Until then, treat any bounce as tactical rather than a new trend, with the Saudi Energy sector offering the most defensible near-term exposure given oil's bid.

What to Watch Next Week

The week of July 13-17 is among the most data-dense of the year and could materially reprice multiple asset classes simultaneously. Tuesday's U.S. CPI report and Fed Chair Warsh's House testimony are the twin anchors: a hot inflation print combined with any hawkish signalling from Warsh would pressure bonds and growth equities together, the most damaging combination for portfolio positioning. Wednesday brings PPI and Warsh's Senate appearance, along with ASML's earnings, and Thursday delivers TSMC results alongside retail sales and weekly jobless claims. On the earnings side, the major U.S. banks report Tuesday through Wednesday, including JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, setting the tone for financials sector sentiment and providing the first systematic read on consumer credit health. For Pakistan, the focus shifts to June quarter corporate results, which are expected to provide positive earnings surprises particularly in cement and E&P. In Saudi Arabia, whether TASI can achieve a sustained close above 10,950 on recovering volume will determine whether the recent consolidation marks a base or a pause before further weakness. And on the geopolitical front, indirect U.S.-Iran talks via Qatar continue, but the probability of a near-term resolution looks poor; any further escalation in Hormuz shipping disruptions remains the single most potent tail risk for oil prices, bonds, and emerging market import-dependent economies in the week ahead.

title: Rotation Nation: Oil, Inflation, and the AI Fracture Define a Pivotal Week
excerpt: A collapsing oil price, fracturing AI trade, and powerful broad-market rotation set the agenda as H2 2026 begins in earnest.
content:
The week ending June 27 delivered a market that was less a single story and more a set of competing gravitational forces pulling capital in different directions simultaneously. A collapsing oil price, the highest U.S. inflation reading since 2023, a hawkish new Federal Reserve chair, a rotting AI consensus, and a quietly strengthening broad market beneath the headline indices all competed for attention. The net result is a global setup where the index-level picture obscures more than it reveals: beneath a flat-to-down S&P 500 and a tumbling Nasdaq, a genuine rotation is underway, one that carries real investment implications heading into the second half of 2026.

The AI Trade Fractures, but the Market Doesn't Break

The dominant narrative this week was not the collapse of the AI trade but its fracturing into something more complex and selective. The Nasdaq Composite fell sharply, losing over 1,200 points on the week and sitting up just 8.84% year-to-date, while three of the Magnificent Seven names are down more than 15% for the year. Nvidia and Broadcom have each shed roughly 10% over the past month, and CoreWeave dropped more than 15% in a single week. The headline catalyst was a cocktail of concerns: reports that OpenAI may delay its IPO to 2027, Apple announcing meaningful price increases across its product lineup, Microsoft citing component inflation in raising Xbox prices, and a growing volume of anecdotal evidence that enterprise AI token spending is blowing through budgets, prompting pullbacks. The Micron earnings episode crystallized the tension well. The memory company posted genuinely extraordinary numbers, with margins expanding sharply as the AI-driven memory bottleneck accreted fully to its income statement. Yet the very strength of those margins triggered bearish concern: historically elevated memory prices historically invite engineering workarounds, a pivot to lower-cost open-source models, and eventually the economic axiom that the cure for high prices is high prices.

What matters for portfolio construction is what sits beneath these headlines. The equal-weighted S&P 500 outperformed its market-cap-weighted peer by roughly 350 basis points on the week. Small caps continued their remarkable run, with the Russell 2000 up over 21% year-to-date versus less than 8% for the headline S&P 500. Seven of eleven S&P sectors finished the week higher. Healthcare led, recovering from being down roughly 5% on the year, with Eli Lilly rising more than 6% in a single session. REITs, consumer staples, and utilities also advanced. The market is not broken. It is rotating, and that rotation is gathering momentum.

Oil's Collapse and Its Disinflation Dividend

The most underappreciated macro development of recent weeks is the speed and scale of oil's decline. WTI is now trading below $70 per barrel, down nearly $25 from a month ago and more than $40 from its 2026 peak. The driver is the interim U.S.-Iran peace deal that has held long enough to allow tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz to recover meaningfully, with supply ramping back toward pre-conflict levels. The Brent crude settlement near $72 per barrel reflects a market that is still pricing some geopolitical risk premium, but the direction of travel is unmistakable.

The macroeconomic implications are significant and underpriced in our view. Energy prices alone added a full 1.5 percentage points to headline CPI in May. A sustained move to current oil levels should reverse a meaningful portion of that contribution through the summer and into autumn, offering a genuine disinflation tailwind that markets have not yet fully discounted. National average gasoline prices have already fallen to approximately $3.90 per gallon and are likely to continue lower. For U.S. households, which absorbed the inflation shock this spring by drawing down savings to a 3% savings rate while still growing consumption at a 2.1% annualized pace over the three months through May, cheaper fuel is genuine relief. The risk is not the oil decline itself but the geopolitical fragility underpinning it: any renewed interruption to Hormuz traffic would reverse much of this gain rapidly.

Inflation, the Fed, and the Rate Calculus

The PCE data released this week confirmed that headline U.S. inflation has accelerated to 4.1% year-over-year in May, the highest reading since April 2023, while core PCE reached 3.4%, its highest since October 2023. These are not comfortable numbers for a central bank already signaling hawkish intent. New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first policy meeting produced a hold at the current range of 3.5% to 3.75%, but the tone was unambiguously hawkish, with half of the FOMC penciling rate hikes into their projections. Treasury yields fell on the week as oil dropped and the PCE print came in roughly in line with expectations, with the 10-year note breaking below 4.40% for the first time in over a month. But the underlying policy trajectory remains biased toward tightening rather than easing.

The critical question for the second half is whether the oil-driven disinflation materializes fast enough to allow the Fed to stay on hold through year-end. Our read is that it probably does, but with little margin for error. Core PCE at 3.4% is well above the Fed's 2% target, and wage pressures remain firm. The labor market picture next week, including job openings, ADP, Challenger Gray, and the official payroll report, will be pivotal. A strong labor print would reignite hike expectations; a softer one would reinforce the on-hold base case. The Consumer Sentiment Index's upward revision to 49.5 for June, driven by cheaper fuel costs, suggests households are beginning to notice the oil decline, but the 4.6% one-year inflation expectation embedded in the same survey tells us the inflation psychology has not yet broken.

Europe: Oil Helps, Politics Complicates

The eurozone composite PMI edged up to 49.5 in June, its highest since March and slightly above expectations, but this masks significant divergence. Germany's composite PMI fell to 48.0, its third consecutive monthly decline, with respondents citing deteriorating conditions and elevated uncertainty. The STOXX Europe 600 ended the week essentially flat, with Germany's DAX down 1.26% and Italy's FTSE MIB falling 3.00%, while the UK's FTSE 100 gained 1.40%. Eurozone consumer inflation expectations declined to 3.5% for the next twelve months in the ECB's latest survey, the lowest in three months, driven in part by lower oil prices. That directionally helpful shift should temper pressure on the ECB to hike further, though the institution has already delivered a 25 basis point increase and markets have pared expectations for additional moves.

The UK added a layer of political complexity with Prime Minister Keir Starmer's resignation following months of pressure, with the Labour Party now expected to coalesce around Andy Burnham as successor. UK retail sales volumes dropped to a weighted balance of -54 in June, down from -46 in May, while manufacturing order books hit their worst level since 2020. The pound remains close to multi-year support levels against the dollar. European equity exposure looks selectively interesting given valuations, but the German drag and UK political transition argue for patience before adding aggressively.

Japan and Asia: Yen Pressure, Inflation Signals

Japan's markets declined through the week, with the Nikkei 225 losing 2.65% and the TOPIX shedding 2.02%, caught in the same global technology selloff that weighed on semiconductors globally. The yen continued its drift toward the high end of the 161 range against the dollar, a level that has historically attracted intervention speculation. Tokyo CPI accelerated in June to 1.7% year-over-year, with the measure excluding food and energy rising to 1.9%, signaling that imported energy inflation is beginning to broaden into core goods and services. The Bank of Japan is expected to continue gradual rate normalization, which in the context of a still-weak yen creates an ongoing tension between the currency defense imperative and the institution's cautious policy pace. The Korean market experienced a circuit breaker event earlier in the week, a reminder that Asia ex-Japan remains susceptible to sharp local dislocations. Singapore's industrial production contracted in May, dragged by pharmaceuticals and medical technology, though electronics and precision engineering remained strong.

Crypto: ETF Outflows Slow, but the Bid Remains Thin

Bitcoin is ending the week at approximately $59,851, down 1.53% over the past 24 hours and the second time this month it has traded below $60,000. Ethereum sits at $1,578, Solana at $71.77, and BNB at $554. The weekly pattern is consistent with what we flagged in the daily briefs throughout the week: crypto is not the leading risk asset in this environment. Capital is rotating toward AI tech, small caps, and cyclicals rather than digital assets, and the hawkish Fed posture combined with a stronger dollar creates structural headwinds for Bitcoin specifically. Bitcoin ETF outflows have now extended to six consecutive weeks, with another $228 million exiting U.S. spot products in the latest week. The more constructive signal is the pace: the prior four weeks each saw outflows exceeding $1 billion, each week worse than the last. The deceleration suggests the forced selling may be transitioning toward patience, but it does not yet constitute a buy signal. CNN's Fear and Greed Index is reading Extreme Fear for U.S. markets broadly, a contrarian indicator, though the crypto-specific setup requires more than sentiment reversal to drive a meaningful recovery while dollar strength persists.

Pakistan and the Gulf: Frontier and Emerging Market Snapshots

The KSE-100 in Pakistan closed at 179,571 points, up 0.36% on the week, supported by geopolitical easing following the signing of a peace memorandum of understanding and driven by strong contributions from E&P names including OGDC and PPL. The index trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of 8.3x with a 6.1% dividend yield, making it one of the highest-yielding and lowest-valued markets in the regional comparison universe. Fuel price cuts this week, with motor spirit down PKR 74 per liter and high-speed diesel down PKR 67 per liter, are meaningful for consumer purchasing power in an oil-importing economy. T-Bill cut-off yields fell 39 to 115 basis points in the latest auction, a signal of easing monetary conditions. The Saudi TASI, meanwhile, closed at 10,933, down 1.69% on the week, with the index now sitting just above the key 10,900 support level. The technical picture has deteriorated, with the RSI falling to 39, price trading below both the 20-day moving average and the point of control at 11,025, and volume declining sharply. A confirmed recovery above 11,025 to 11,050 is needed before the constructive case can be re-established.

This Week's Recommendations

  • Add to equal-weight and small-cap U.S. equity exposure. With the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforming the cap-weighted index by roughly 350 basis points on the week and the Russell 2000 up over 21% year-to-date versus less than 8% for the headline S&P 500, the rotation out of mega-cap tech into broader market exposure is real and supported by fundamentals. The breadth of this move, seven of eleven sectors positive on the week, is not a defensive rotation. It reflects improving earnings across the market. July is historically the strongest month for the S&P 500, averaging over 3% gains in the past decade with no negative years in that window.
  • Remain underweight long-duration tech and AI infrastructure names. The fracturing of the AI trade is not a one-week phenomenon. With Nvidia and Broadcom each down roughly 10% over the past month, software ETFs approaching mid-April lows, and the OpenAI IPO reportedly pushed to 2027, the near-term catalyst for a reversal is unclear. The memory price cycle also argues for caution: elevated DRAM pricing historically triggers engineering workarounds and model efficiency improvements that reduce demand. Hold existing positions in companies with genuine earnings delivery, but new capital is better deployed in the rotation trades than in AI infrastructure at current levels.
  • Consider selective investment-grade corporate bond exposure. Treasury yields declined on the week, with the 10-year breaking below 4.40%, and investment-grade corporate issues were on average oversubscribed in new issuance. The combination of a Fed on hold, decelerating energy-driven inflation, and solid economic growth tracked at approximately 2.5% annualized in Q2 supports the spread compression case. High yield is less compelling, with pressure from heavy new issuance, slowing fund inflows, and risk-off sentiment around AI equity valuations.
  • Watch Pakistan's E&P sector for frontier exposure. OGDC and PPL contributed meaningfully to the KSE-100's positive week, and new gas production from the Sahito-1 and Shams-1 wells adds to domestic supply in an energy-import-sensitive economy. The index's 8.3x P/E and 6.1% dividend yield represent compelling value on a regional comparison basis, particularly as the peace MOU and fuel price cuts improve the near-term macro backdrop. Position sizing should remain modest given liquidity constraints, but the risk-reward is favorable for investors with appropriate frontier market tolerance.
  • Hold cash or very short duration on crypto. Bitcoin at $59,851, Ethereum at $1,578, and Solana at $71.77 are all in structurally weak territory. Six consecutive weeks of ETF outflows, a hawkish Fed, a stronger dollar, and capital rotating toward AI tech equities rather than digital assets create a poor setup for meaningful near-term recovery. The slowdown in ETF outflow pace is a watch signal, not a buy signal. Re-entry looks more compelling if BTC can reclaim $62,000 to $65,000 on volume, or if the Fed pivots meaningfully on rate hike guidance in response to labor market softening.

What to Watch Next Week

The holiday-shortened week ahead is packed with labor market data that will define the Fed's path for the rest of the summer. Job openings, ADP private payrolls, Challenger Gray layoff data, weekly unemployment claims, and the official government employment report are all due within a compressed window. A strong labor print would revive rate hike expectations and pressure equities and bonds simultaneously. A soft one would validate the on-hold case and likely extend the small-cap and equal-weight rally. Beyond labor, watch Hormuz tanker traffic and oil price direction closely: any sign of renewed geopolitical tension in the Strait would reverse the disinflation tailwind that is currently supporting both consumer sentiment and bond prices. In Saudi Arabia, whether the TASI can reclaim the 11,025 to 11,050 zone on stronger volume will determine whether last week's decline was a failed breakdown or the start of a more sustained move toward the 10,750 support level. In crypto, the pace of Bitcoin ETF outflows in the coming week will tell us whether the deceleration observed over the past two weeks is the beginning of stabilization or a temporary pause before another leg lower.

Markets at a Crossroads: Compression, Catalysts, and Cautious Optimism

The week ending 18 June delivered a quietly constructive set of signals across emerging and frontier markets, but the dominant theme was compression: compressed volatility in Saudi equities, compressed crypto momentum after a strong early-week move, and compressed valuation spreads across regional emerging markets that continue to make certain names look compellingly cheap against global peers. Nothing broke out definitively, and that in itself is the story. When markets sit this coiled, the next directional move tends to be sharp. The data this week gives us enough to sharpen both our conviction levels and our risk triggers across geographies.

Saudi Arabia: The Coil Tightens at 11,121

TASI closed the week at 11,121, up 79 points or 0.72%, marking a second consecutive weekly advance and a successful defence of the key volume-at-price floor near 11,025. That level has now been tested and held repeatedly, making it arguably the most important single support level in the current structure. What is technically striking this week is not the advance itself but the Bollinger Band picture: bandwidth sits at just 2%, one of the tightest compression readings in recent memory, while %B has climbed to approximately 85%, placing price firmly in the upper portion of those bands. History is clear on what this combination tends to produce: a sharp, fast directional move once the trigger arrives.

The resistance picture is equally well-defined. TASI is now probing the 11,150 to 11,200 zone, which sits at the lower end of a denser volume node extending to 11,270. The RSI at 54 and the emerging +DI over -DI crossover are constructive without being overextended, but ADX at approximately 17 tells us this is still an early-trend environment, not a confirmed breakout. Weekly traded value dipped 4.7% to SAR 26.2 billion, a reminder that participation remains thin and that any bullish resolution will require volume to show up. A confirmed close above 11,200 on expanding turnover is the line to watch. A loss of 11,025 flips the picture back toward 10,900.

At the sector level, the breadth was broad: 150 names advanced versus 105 declining, with Transportation, Software and Services, Consumer Services, Pharma, and Healthcare leading. Energy was the notable laggard, down 2.5% on the week, consistent with the softer crude backdrop. The week's most interesting single-stock move was FLYNAS, up 15.3%, alongside Saudi Arabian Mining (Ma'aden) gaining 9.8% on both price and significantly elevated trading value of SAR 1.19 billion, suggesting institutional positioning rather than retail momentum. On the downside, Kingdom Holding fell 11.8% and Rabigh Refining dropped 11%, both worth monitoring as they reflect continued pressure on the petrochemical and holding-company segments of the market.

Pakistan: Budget Buzz Lifts KSE-100, But Geopolitics Keep a Hand on the Brake

The KSE-100 had a genuinely strong week, closing at 178,923 points, up 3.79% week-on-week, adding 6,523 points. The early-week catalyst was the federal budget announcement and anticipation of a peace-related memorandum of understanding, which drove a sharp rally. That momentum reversed partially late in the week following reports of ceasefire violations, producing an intraday correction that trimmed what had looked like an even more impressive gain. The two forces, domestic fiscal optimism and regional security uncertainty, are likely to remain in tension through the near term.

The macro backdrop is mixed but not unfavourable. The State Bank of Pakistan held its policy rate at 11.5%, a decision that reflects the balancing act between still-elevated inflation and slowing economic activity. Large-scale manufacturing output grew 6.1% year-on-year in April, and technology exports reached USD 373 million, representing 45% of total services exports, a structural positive for the economy's long-term composition. Pakistan's current account swung to a surplus of USD 459 million in May, a meaningful improvement from a USD 44 million deficit a year earlier, though cumulative 11-month figures show the surplus has narrowed sharply from prior-year levels. Liquid foreign exchange reserves rose to USD 22.7 billion as of 18 June, providing approximately 2.71 months of import cover.

The valuation story remains KSE-100's most powerful argument. At a forward P/E of 8.3x and a dividend yield of 6.1%, the index is the cheapest and highest-yielding market in the regional comparison this week by a material margin. Return on equity of 19% is the highest in the peer group surveyed, against a P/B of just 1.6x, a combination that screams mispricing relative to fundamentals if the geopolitical risk premium ever normalises. Average daily volumes surged 47.8% week-on-week, and average daily traded value rose 118% to USD 226 million, suggesting that domestic and institutional conviction is building. The PIB auction, which saw the government raise PKR 649 billion against a PKR 350 billion target with yields declining across the curve, adds another constructive data point: fixed income markets are signalling confidence in the fiscal trajectory.

Crypto: Consolidation in the $63K-$65K Band Defines the Week

Bitcoin spent the week oscillating between roughly USD 63,870 and USD 67,000, ultimately settling around USD 64,105 as of Sunday morning, up 0.51% in the past 24 hours. The pattern across the week was a familiar one: a move toward USD 67,000 early in the week, then a gradual retreat as risk appetite cooled toward the end. Ethereum slipped from USD 1,775 to USD 1,733, continuing its underperformance relative to Bitcoin in recent weeks. Solana was the most interesting mover as of Sunday, up 3.38% in 24 hours to USD 74.08, consistent with its pattern of sharper short-term swings around the group mean.

The weekly brief coverage highlighted VC funding surging in the crypto and fintech space and Revolut expanding into the UAE, both of which speak to the structural adoption narrative that underpins the medium-term bull case for digital assets. The concern for near-term Bitcoin traders is that the USD 63,000 to USD 65,000 range has now acted as both support and resistance over multiple sessions, and a clean directional break in either direction is overdue. The Iran-related geopolitical developments flagged in the Pakistan commentary are also worth watching for their knock-on effect on risk appetite globally, including crypto markets, where sentiment can shift quickly when macro uncertainty rises.

Regional Valuation Landscape: Where the Value Is

Stepping back across the regional comparison data available this week, the valuation dispersion between markets is striking. Pakistan at 8.3x P/E and 6.1% dividend yield anchors the cheap end of the spectrum. Saudi Arabia at 17.3x P/E and a broadly diversified sector mix sits in the moderate valuation range for an oil-linked economy with Vision 2030 tailwinds. The TASI market cap sits at SAR 9.6 trillion with solid banking representation, and the sector P/E table shows Pharma and Healthcare trading at 21.7x and 25.6x respectively, which is reasonable given the growth profile of healthcare spending in the Kingdom.

The comparison across Asian markets is also worth noting. Taiwan and South Korea lead on P/E multiples but offer dividend yields below 2%, making them expensive for income-focused allocators. India's 22x P/E and 1.5x P/B remain elevated relative to both Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. For a cross-market allocator, the combination of Pakistan's extreme value, improving macro, and high domestic institutional activity, alongside Saudi Arabia's technically coiled setup and structural reform catalysts, offers a genuinely interesting dual-market emerging-market position heading into the second half of 2026.

This Week's Recommendations

  • TASI tactical long on breakout confirmation: Hold a measured long bias on TASI with a clear trigger: a volume-backed close above 11,200 opens the path to 11,250 to 11,300. Keep the stop below 11,025, the POC that has now been defended twice. Do not chase the move before confirmation given the tight Bollinger Band setup and the risk of a false breakout in either direction.
  • Ma'aden (Saudi Arabian Mining, 1211) as a high-conviction TASI name: The 9.8% weekly gain accompanied by SAR 1.19 billion in traded value signals institutional accumulation rather than retail noise. With the Materials sector up 2.4% on the week and a longer-term YTD gain of 6.2%, the technical and flow picture supports holding or adding on pullbacks toward the mid-50s range.
  • KSE-100 selective exposure via domestic-demand and E&P names: For investors with emerging-market appetite, the KSE-100 at 8.3x P/E and 6.1% yield with 19% ROE is a structurally compelling value case. The week's top point contributors, UBL in banks, ENGROH, HUBC, PPL, and OGDC in energy and fertiliser, represent the sectors with the clearest fundamental anchors. Geopolitical noise around ceasefire violations is real, but the macro trajectory, reserves building, current account in surplus, PIB auction oversubscribed, is pointing in the right direction. Size positions accordingly given the binary event risk.
  • Bitcoin: hold the range, watch USD 63,000 as the key support: The USD 63,000 to USD 65,000 band has absorbed selling pressure multiple times this week. A sustained break below USD 63,000 would shift the near-term bias negative and warrant reducing exposure. Conversely, a clean move above USD 67,000 on volume would reopen the USD 70,000 conversation. For now, this is a range-hold rather than a directional trade.
  • Solana as the higher-beta crypto expression: SOL's 3.38% Sunday move and its consistent pattern of amplifying directional moves relative to BTC and ETH make it the most interesting expression of a bullish crypto view for investors who already hold core Bitcoin. A base near USD 70 to USD 72 has been building; the risk is a sharp reversal if broader risk appetite deteriorates on macro grounds.

What to Watch Next Week

The most important single variable for Saudi Arabia next week is whether TASI can push through and close convincingly above 11,200 on meaningful volume. The Bollinger compression cannot persist indefinitely, and the next week or two is likely to resolve the direction. Watch daily traded value for any pickup above SAR 6 billion per session as a signal that institutional conviction is returning.

For Pakistan, the Muharram public holidays shorten the trading week, which will dampen volume and may exaggerate intraday moves. The more critical variable is whether the geopolitical situation around the India-Pakistan border stabilises or deteriorates further. Any escalation would undo the fiscal optimism that drove this week's rally; any de-escalation or signed peace MoU would likely unlock another sharp leg higher given the valuation starting point.

On crypto, the US-Iran conflict developments flagged in this week's data will matter for risk appetite broadly, with knock-on effects for digital assets. The week's VC funding momentum and fintech expansion news, particularly Revolut in the UAE, point to structural adoption continuing regardless of price action, but price action in the near term will be driven by macro sentiment. Watch for any Bitcoin move outside the USD 63,000 to USD 67,000 range as the directional trigger for the next trade. Global coverage on European markets and US equities was limited in this week's research inputs, so we will update those views as material becomes available through the daily brief cycle.
